variants.name: enum.Enum with auto() and @unique
variants.idiom_name: enum.Enum module class (members are singletons, not values)
variants.implementation_notes: The stdlib enum module provides the pattern: a class deriving from Enum declares one singleton member per constant, members are not equal to their values and cannot be compared across types, and @unique rejects duplicate values while auto() assigns them. The classic private-constructor structure is unnecessary - the metaclass does the instance control and iteration - so this is the default; reserve IntEnum/StrEnum for interoperating with existing primitive constants.
variants.code_sketch:
from enum import Enum, unique

@unique
class Suit(Enum):
    CLUBS = "clubs"
    DIAMONDS = "diamonds"
    HEARTS = "hearts"
    SPADES = "spades"

Suit("clubs")           # -> Suit.CLUBS; unknown labels raise ValueError
Suit.CLUBS == "clubs"   # False: members never equal their raw values
pitfalls: Without @unique two names may share one value (aliases), silently collapsing members.
Pickling and JSON round-trips go through member names, so renaming a member breaks persisted data.
Reassigning a module-level member name is not a rebind of the enum member; mutation of enum state needs care in subclasses (use the stdlib patterns, not ad-hoc mutation).

variants.name: IntEnum / StrEnum drop-in constants
variants.implementation_notes: When replacing existing integer or string constants that must keep working with raw values (DB rows, wire payloads, comparison against literals), IntEnum and StrEnum deliberately re-open interoperability: members are instances of int/str, compare equal to their values, and primitive operations return plain primitives. Choose this variant for migration and boundary code, not for the domain core; StrEnum requires Python 3.11+, IntEnum exists since the enum module (3.4).
variants.code_sketch:
from enum import StrEnum

class Suit(StrEnum):
    CLUBS = "clubs"
    DIAMONDS = "diamonds"

Suit.CLUBS == "clubs"   # True: deliberately interoperable with str
str(Suit.CLUBS)         # 'clubs' (the value, not 'Suit.CLUBS')
pitfalls: Equality with raw primitives reopens exactly the mixing the pattern exists to prevent; a typo'd string compares unequal, but any string can be compared.
Mixed-in members are singletons by identity while == accepts the primitive: code that uses `is` and code that uses == disagree.
Operations on members (int arithmetic, str concatenation) return plain primitives, silently losing membership; use Flag/IntFlag when set arithmetic is the domain.
